title: Course Schedule III
statement:
There are `n` courses. Course `i` takes `duration[i]` consecutive days and must be **finished** no later than day `lastDay[i]`; finishing exactly on day `lastDay[i]` is allowed.

You can study only one course at a time and must finish a course once you start it. You begin on day 1, so if you take courses back to back, the course that ends after total `T` days of study finishes on day `T`. A course counts only if it finishes by its own last day.

You may skip any courses. Find the **maximum number of courses** you can complete.

A tempting solution sorts by deadline and takes every course that still fits, but that can lock in a long course early on. The correct approach must be able to undo such a choice.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `duration[i]` and `lastDay[i]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum number of courses that can be completed.

examples.explanation: Take the courses with (duration, last day) of (1, 2), (2, 5) and (4, 9): they finish on days 1, 3 and 7, all within their last days. Taking all four needs 10 days, which breaks the last day 9 of the final course, so 3 is the maximum.
The only course needs 5 days but must finish by day 3, so it can never be completed.
Taking them in order of last day they finish on days 2, 4 and 6, each exactly on its last day.

hints: Only the set of chosen courses matters, because within a chosen set the best order is by increasing last day. So process courses sorted by last day.
Add each course to the plan. If the total duration now exceeds the current course's last day, the plan is infeasible.

To repair an infeasible plan, drop the course with the longest duration so far (it may be the one just added). A max-heap of chosen durations makes this O(log n), and dropping the longest never reduces the count more than necessary.
